comm.label: Communication
comm.description: speaks clearly and fluently at a steady pace, with confidence and good structure

levels.1: Hard to follow: disorganised, very short or rambling, little sense of the listener.
levels.3: Clear enough with some structure; mostly relevant; uses a reasonable share of the time.
levels.5: Clear, well organised and engaging from start to finish; signposts points, adapts language to the listener and finishes on time.

equity.label: Equity and social justice
equity.description: aware of fairness, social justice and human rights in health; can explain how discrimination and social determinants create and maintain inequities

levels.1: Does not notice unfairness, or blames individuals for structural problems.
levels.3: Recognises that some groups are affected more and names one or two causes.
levels.5: Explains several structural causes (discrimination, social determinants, access), who is affected and why, and suggests fair, practical responses.

ethics.label: Ethical reasoning
ethics.description: sees more than one side of an issue and applies ethical principles with integrity to reach a fair, reasoned position

levels.1: Gives a one-sided or unreasoned view; misses the dilemma.
levels.3: Identifies the main dilemma and considers more than one side.
levels.5: Weighs competing principles and stakeholders fairly, reaches a reasoned position and acknowledges its limits.

critical.label: Critical thinking
critical.description: identifies the real issue, analyses it, draws logical unbiased conclusions and builds a structured, persuasive argument

levels.1: Restates the question or makes assertions without reasons.
levels.3: Identifies the main issue and gives some reasons and examples.
levels.5: Analyses the issue in depth, weighs evidence and trade-offs, and builds a logical, persuasive argument.

cultural.label: Cultural safety and self-reflection
cultural.description: recognises how their own culture and background shape their view, respects other perspectives and is willing to learn from them

levels.1: Shows little awareness of their own perspective or of other cultures; may stereotype.
levels.3: Shows some awareness that culture and background shape views; respectful.
levels.5: Reflects honestly on their own culturally shaped perspective, shows genuine respect and curiosity about others, and links this to safe care.

team.label: Teamwork and leadership
team.description: draws on real experience of diverse teams: taking initiative, building trust, handling conflict, shared accountability

levels.1: No concrete example, or describes teamwork only in general terms.
levels.3: Gives a relevant example with a clear role and some reflection.
levels.5: Gives a specific example showing initiative, trust-building, handling conflict and shared accountability, with clear lessons learned.

resilience.label: Resilience and motivation
resilience.description: handles setbacks constructively, shows realistic motivation for a health career, a growth mindset and deliberate self-care

levels.1: Little evidence of coping or motivation; vague or unrealistic.
levels.3: Describes a real challenge and reasonable coping or motivation.
levels.5: Shows realistic understanding of challenges, specific coping and self-care strategies already used, growth from setbacks and well-grounded motivation.

flex.label: Flexible problem solving
flex.description: thinks fluently, combines ideas in new ways and suggests creative, practical solutions

levels.1: No solutions, or only one obvious idea.
levels.5: Generates several creative, practical ideas, adapts when considering new angles and is open to changing their mind.

domains: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

stations.title: Should Medicare cover teeth?
stations.scenario: In Australia, public dental care for adults is generally only available to concession card holders, and waiting lists can be long. Most adults pay for dental care themselves.
stations.question: Should Medicare cover dental care for all adults? What are the arguments on each side?
keyPoints: Links oral health to general health, pain, nutrition, work and self-esteem
Equity: cost barriers fall hardest on lower-income, rural and remote, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
Arguments for: prevention, fewer emergency and hospital admissions, fairness
Arguments against or limits: cost, workforce, competing priorities
Middle options: expanding concession eligibility, prevention in schools, community clinics, staged rollout
Reasoned conclusion that acknowledges trade-offs

stations.title: The city–country divide
stations.scenario: People living in rural and remote Australia generally have lower life expectancy and less access to health services than people in major cities.
stations.question: What causes this gap, and what could help close it?
keyPoints: Causes: distance, workforce shortages, fewer specialists, cost of travel, higher-risk jobs, ageing populations
Higher proportion of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in remote areas
Solutions: rural training pathways, incentives, telehealth, outreach, Royal Flying Doctor Service-style models, nurse practitioners
Community-led and local solutions
Recognises no single fix; long-term investment
Clear, structured argument

stations.title: Navigating the NDIS
stations.scenario: The National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) supports hundreds of thousands of Australians with disability, but many people find it hard to apply for and use.
stations.question: Who might miss out, and how could access be made fairer?
keyPoints: Groups at risk: people with complex needs, low literacy, limited English, rural and remote residents, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, people without advocates
Barriers: paperwork, evidence requirements, cost of assessments, digital access
Ideas: navigators and advocates, simpler processes, outreach, culturally safe services
Co-design with people with disability
Balances sustainability of the scheme with fairness
Respectful, non-deficit language

stations.title: Starting again
stations.scenario: People who come to Australia as refugees may face language barriers, past trauma and a health system that works very differently from the one they knew.
stations.question: What challenges might they face, and how could health services help?
keyPoints: Challenges: language, unfamiliar system, cost, transport, trauma, mistrust, cultural expectations
Health needs: untreated conditions, mental health, vaccinations, dental care
Trauma-informed and culturally safe care
Practical help: free interpreters, refugee health services, community health workers, longer appointments
Partnership with settlement services and communities
Recognises strengths and resilience

stations.title: Many languages
stations.scenario: More than one in five Australians speak a language other than English at home.
stations.question: What does this mean for health care, and what should health services do?
keyPoints: Risks: misunderstanding, poor informed consent, medicine errors, missed follow-up
Problems with using family members, especially children, as interpreters
Professional interpreters (phone, video, in person), translated materials, bilingual staff
Cultural beliefs about health and illness
Health literacy and teach-back
Practical and respectful suggestions

stations.title: The cost of seeing a GP
stations.scenario: From November 2025, the federal government extended bulk billing incentives to all Medicare-eligible patients, but many people still pay out-of-pocket costs for some health care.
stations.question: Who is most affected by out-of-pocket costs, and what else could improve access?
keyPoints: Groups affected: low-income households, people with chronic conditions, rural residents, young adults, people needing specialists or allied health
Effects: delayed care, more emergency department visits, worse chronic disease control
Recognises bulk billing alone does not fix workforce shortages or specialist costs
Other levers: nurse practitioners, community health centres, telehealth, urgent care clinics
Trade-offs: cost to government, GP viability
Reasoned opinion

stations.title: No fixed address
stations.scenario: People experiencing homelessness often have serious health problems and frequently rely on emergency departments for care.
stations.question: Why might this happen, and what would a better approach look like?
keyPoints: Barriers: no Medicare card or ID, cost, no phone, mistrust, competing survival needs
Health issues: chronic illness, mental health, injuries, substance use
Better approaches: outreach clinics, street health teams, housing-first, integrated services
Dignity and non-judgemental care
Cost-effectiveness of prevention versus emergency care
Practical, compassionate answer

stations.title: Years to a diagnosis
stations.scenario: Endometriosis is common, yet many women in Australia report waiting years for a diagnosis, and say their pain was dismissed.
stations.question: Why might this happen, and what could be done?
keyPoints: Bias: normalising period pain, gender stereotypes, historic research based on men
Intersecting factors: cultural background, rurality, cost of specialists
Impacts: suffering, missed school and work, fertility concerns, loss of trust
Solutions: education, listening and believing patients, clearer pathways, specialist clinics
Self-reflection on how their own assumptions could affect how they listen
Structured argument

stations.title: A matter of conscience
stations.scenario: Voluntary assisted dying is now legal in every Australian state and the ACT, but not the Northern Territory. Health practitioners can choose not to take part because of their beliefs.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on health professionals being able to opt out of some kinds of care for personal reasons?
keyPoints: Respects practitioner conscience and moral integrity
Weighs patient rights to lawful care and timely access
Access problems if many opt out, especially in rural areas or faith-based facilities
Duty to give patients information on where to get help (required in most jurisdictions)
Acknowledges diverse religious, cultural and personal views
Reasoned position; not judged on which view they hold

stations.title: Opt-in or opt-out?
stations.scenario: Australia uses an opt-in organ donor register, and families are always asked before donation goes ahead. Only about a third of Australians aged 16 and over are registered.
stations.question: Should Australia move to an opt-out system?
keyPoints: Dilemma: saving lives versus autonomy and genuine consent
Evidence: family consent rates and conversations matter as much as the law
Families are still asked in most opt-out countries
Cultural and religious perspectives, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander views
Alternatives: more registration, family conversations, trained donation specialists
Balanced, reasoned conclusion

stations.title: Paying plasma donors
stations.scenario: Australian blood and plasma donors are unpaid volunteers, but Australia imports a large and growing share of its plasma products from countries that pay donors.
stations.question: Should Australia pay people to donate plasma?
keyPoints: Dilemma: supply and self-sufficiency versus altruism and possible exploitation
Payment could target people on low incomes
Safety concerns about people hiding risk factors
Inconsistency: we already rely on paid donors overseas
Middle options: expenses, time-off schemes, recognition, better access to donor centres
Reasoned conclusion

stations.title: Should parents be told?
stations.scenario: In Australia, young people can often consent to their own health care if they understand it, and from age 15 they can get their own Medicare card.
stations.question: Should parents always be told when their 15-year-old sees a GP?
keyPoints: Tension: young person's privacy and autonomy versus parents' role and protection
Confidentiality encourages young people to seek help early
Limits: serious risk of harm may justify sharing
Encourage involving family where safe
Different family and cultural expectations
Nuanced position

stations.title: Doctors on strike
stations.scenario: In April 2025, thousands of NSW public hospital doctors went on a three-day strike over pay and conditions, the first statewide doctors' strike in decades. Earlier that year, many public psychiatrists resigned.
stations.question: Should doctors be allowed to strike?
keyPoints: Workers' rights and the link between staffing, fatigue and patient safety
Duty of care and risk to patients during action
Emergency and life-preserving cover
Long-term effects on retention if conditions do not improve
Who is most affected by disruption
Balanced position

stations.title: A gift of thanks
stations.scenario: A grateful patient offers their GP an expensive gift after treatment.
stations.question: Should health professionals accept gifts from patients?
keyPoints: Value and timing matter
Risks: favouritism, pressure, conflict of interest, vulnerable patients
Cultural meaning of gifts; refusing can offend
Professional guidance and declaring gifts
Options: decline graciously, share with team, donate
Balanced answer

stations.title: Hidden in the food
stations.scenario: A woman with advanced dementia in an aged care home often refuses her medicines. A staff member suggests hiding them in her food.
stations.question: What are your thoughts?
keyPoints: Tension between wellbeing and autonomy and dignity
Capacity and who decides (substitute decision-maker)
Explore why she refuses
Proper process: assessment, family or guardian involvement, documented plan
Alternatives and medication review first
Links to concerns about quality of aged care

stations.title: Should the family know?
stations.scenario: A genetic test shows a patient carries a gene variant that greatly raises the risk of a serious but often preventable cancer. Their siblings may carry it too. The patient does not want them told.
stations.question: What are your thoughts?
keyPoints: Confidentiality and autonomy versus preventing serious harm to relatives
Explore the patient's reasons
Support the patient to tell family
Disclosure without consent needs strong justification and senior advice
Trust in the health system
Balanced conclusion

stations.title: Ambulance ramping
stations.scenario: Ambulance ramping, where patients wait in ambulances outside crowded emergency departments, has been reported in several Australian states.
stations.question: What causes this, and what could help?
keyPoints: Whole-system causes: bed shortages, delayed discharges, aged care and NDIS placement delays, GP access
Impacts: delayed care, ambulances unavailable for new calls, staff burnout
Solutions: urgent care clinics, hospital-in-the-home, faster discharge, more beds and staff, virtual EDs
Equity: effects on rural and older patients
Trade-offs and cost
Clear opinion without needing statistics

stations.title: Vapes behind the counter
stations.scenario: Since July 2024, vapes can only be legally sold in Australian pharmacies, and people under 18 need a prescription. Many young people still vape.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on this approach?
keyPoints: Aims: stop youth uptake while supporting adults quitting smoking
Challenges: illegal supply, enforcement, nicotine addiction already present
Role of pharmacists and GPs in quit support
Education young people trust; involving young people
Equity: uneven effects across communities
Forms and justifies a view

stations.title: Under 16, no account
stations.scenario: Since 10 December 2025, major social media platforms must take reasonable steps to stop Australians under 16 from having accounts.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on this law?
keyPoints: Recognises harms (cyberbullying, comparison, sleep) and benefits (connection, identity, support, especially for isolated young people)
Practical questions: age checks, privacy, workarounds
Effects on rural, disabled and minority young people who rely on online communities
Alternatives or complements: platform safety design, education, parent tools
Evidence still developing; review planned
Balanced, reasoned position

stations.title: Fluoride in the water
stations.scenario: About 90% of Australians drink fluoridated water, but several Queensland councils have recently voted to stop adding fluoride.
stations.question: What are your thoughts?
keyPoints: Evidence that fluoridation reduces tooth decay, especially for children and lower-income communities
Concerns raised: choice, consent, safety worries, misinformation
Who should decide: councils or state government
Equity: regional areas lose more
How to communicate evidence respectfully

stations.title: Taxing sugary drinks
stations.scenario: Many countries tax sugary drinks to reduce obesity and tooth decay. Australia does not have a tax like this.
stations.question: Should Australia introduce one?
keyPoints: Arguments for: overseas evidence of lower consumption, revenue for health
Arguments against: regressive cost, personal freedom, industry impact
Equity: benefits greatest where consumption is highest
Complementary measures: labelling, marketing limits, water in schools
One tax is not a complete solution
Justified view

stations.title: Doctors from overseas
stations.scenario: Australia relies heavily on doctors trained overseas, especially in rural areas, and has introduced faster registration pathways for some of them.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on how Australia should meet its need for doctors?
keyPoints: Benefits of overseas-trained doctors; support they need to settle and practise safely

Training more locally, rural and Indigenous pathways

stations.title: AI in the consulting room

stations.title: Hotter summers

stations.question: How should the health system prepare?
keyPoints: Who is most at risk: older people, people living alone, outdoor workers, people with chronic illness, those without cooling, remote communities
Health system actions: early warnings, checking on vulnerable people, cooling centres, hospital surge plans
Links between climate and health equity
Health sector's own emissions

stations.domain: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
stations.title: Closing the Gap
stations.scenario: In 2020–22, life expectancy for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people was about 8 to 9 years lower than for non-Indigenous Australians. The national Closing the Gap target is to close it by 2031.
stations.question: What factors contribute to this gap?
keyPoints: Colonisation, dispossession from Country, past government policies and intergenerational trauma
Social determinants: income, housing, education, employment, remoteness
Racism in health care and wider society
Access barriers and culturally unsafe services
Strengths: culture, community control, Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations
Avoids blaming individuals

stations.domain: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
stations.title: A preventable disease
stations.scenario: Rates of rheumatic heart disease among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the Northern Territory are among the highest in the world, though the disease is rare elsewhere in Australia.
stations.question: Why might this be, and how could it be prevented?
keyPoints: Basic understanding: follows untreated strep infections of the throat or skin; damages heart valves
Structural causes: crowded housing, poverty, access to primary care in remote areas

Prevention: healthy homes, skin and throat infection care, screening, regular penicillin for those affected
Community-led programs and Aboriginal health workers
Avoids blaming families
